name: Dutch

ancestors.notes: Descent from Proto-Germanic via Old Low Franconian
French adstrate: centuries of Burgundian/French influence in S. Netherlands; cf. van der Wal (2008)

notes: Standard Dutch (ABN / Algemeen Nederlands). ⟨g⟩ realisation is [ɣ] in northern NL and [x] in southern NL / Flanders. /r/ is highly variable. FINAL DEVOICING: b/d/g/v/z devoiced in coda and word-finally. G: voiced [ɣ] onset, voiceless [x] coda — northern Dutch. H: breathy [ɦ]; fully silent in southern dialects. Sources: van Oostendorp (2000), Gussenhoven (1992), Booij (1995). COMPOUND-FINAL SECONDARY STRESS (Booij 1995, ch. 5): non-head members of a compound carry secondary stress and resist the unstressed e -> schwa reduction that a plain unstressed syllable undergoes; the closed set of toponymic/compound-final graphemes ⟨berg⟩/⟨veld⟩/⟨kerk⟩/⟨brecht⟩ is pinned to its unreduced [ɛ] realisation for this reason (Aalbert-style ⟨bert⟩ was left out: wikipron gold is split roughly evenly between [ɛrt] compound forms and [ərt] given-name forms, so no closed rule is safely citable there). ⟨berg⟩/⟨veld⟩ are positionally scoped (positional_graphemes, word_final vs. default) rather than plain unconditional graphemes: a plain grapheme maximal-munch matches inside ordinary inflected forms too (bergen, velden), where the ⟨g⟩/⟨d⟩ is NOT in coda (onset of the following syllable) and must stay voiced per the regular g/d positional rules above -- only word-final ⟨berg⟩/⟨veld⟩ get the devoiced [x]/[t]. ⟨kerk⟩/⟨brecht⟩ need no such split: ⟨k⟩ and ⟨ch⟩ never alternate in Dutch, so the same surface form is correct word-finally and word-internally (kerken, Hubrecht). The adjectival/toponymic suffix ⟨isch⟩ ([-is], ⟨ch⟩ silent, per the existing word-final ⟨sch⟩ -> [s] rule) is likewise pinned as a fixed grapheme rather than derived, since it is a single closed morpheme.

stress.notes: Germanic initial stress default (Booij 1995, ch. 5); the -e(n) verbal/plural ending is unstressed, which is what the open/closed-syllable vowel-length rule and the e -> schwa reduction below need.

allophone_rules.notes: Open-syllable lengthening (Booij 1995, ch. 2): a short vowel letter in an open syllable (single intervocalic consonant, not a doubled/geminate one -- ma-ken not mak-ken) is long. followed_by_2=vowel rules out a doubled consonant letter, since that tokenizes as two consonant graphemes.

Open-syllable lengthening for stressed e (Booij 1995); the unstressed nucleus_unstressed candidate is schwa and is untouched by this rule since it never surfaces as the plain 'e' -> 'ɛ' candidate this rule targets.
Open-syllable lengthening (Booij 1995): u-ren -> [yːrə(n)]/[yrə(n)]; short [ʏ] surfaces only in a closed syllable.

Regressive devoicing assimilation (Booij 1995, ch. 2 sec. 2.5): Dutch obstruents in coda devoice not only word-finally but also before a following voiceless obstruent within the word, e.g. zeg-t [zɛxt], lieg-t [liːxt], hoog-te [ɦoːxtə]. The existing word_final positional override for ⟨g⟩ handles the absolute-final case; this rule extends the same devoicing to pre-obstruent coda position without touching ⟨g⟩ before a sonorant/vowel (dag-je stays [ɣ]: j is not an obstruent).

Unstressed tense vowel (Booij 1995, ch. 2): an unstressed word-final ⟨i⟩ surfaces tense-but-short [i], not lax [ɪ] -- Ali [aːli], Adri [aːdri]. Mirrors the analogous German DE_UNSTRESSED_TENSE_*_FINAL rules (final unstressed high/mid vowels resist laxing).

Unstressed tense vowel in hiatus (Booij 1995, ch. 2): an unstressed ⟨i⟩ directly before another vowel letter (Aziaat, Ariër, Adriaan, -ië/-iër loanword endings) surfaces tense-but-short [i], not lax [ɪ]; the hiatus context blocks the closed-syllable laxing that a following consonant would trigger.
